The train at the edge of the world does not run on coal or electricity. It runs on the quiet inertia of things slipping through the cracks. 

Arthur had been the stationmaster at Terminus Null for what felt like three hundred years, though it was difficult to be certain. The great brass clock suspended above the central concourse had no hands, only a face painted with constellations that shifted gently with the seasons of a sky he could no longer see. Beyond the wrought-iron archways of the platform, there was only the Pale—a thick, luminous fog that smelled faintly of rain on hot pavement and old, unopened letters.

Every day—or whatever passed for a day—Arthur swept the black-and-white checkered tiles with a broom made of birch twigs. He polished the mahogany benches that no one sat upon. And, most importantly, he waited for the whistle.

It was never a loud sound. It was more like the sigh a house makes when it settles in the dead of night, or the hum of a refrigerator noticed only when it suddenly stops. When he heard it, Arthur would set down his broom, adjust his spectacles, and wheel the heavy brass luggage cart out to the yellow line at the edge of Platform One.

The train would emerge from the Pale without the screech of brakes. Its carriages were the color of a bruised plum, its windows dark and reflective. When the doors hissed open, no passengers stepped out. Instead, the porters—shadowy figures made of coats and hats with nothing beneath them—would unload the cargo.

The first carriage always held the physical things. Arthur knew the routine by heart. Crate after crate of single woolen mittens, thousands of cheap plastic pens that still had half their ink, wedding rings that had slipped off fingers in the cold depths of the Atlantic, and keys to doors that had been bulldozed decades ago. Arthur would wheel them into the Great Archive, a labyrinth of towering oak shelves that stretched endlessly into the back of the station, and file them by the date they were last remembered.

It was the second carriage, however, that required a delicate touch. 

The second carriage carried the intangibles. They arrived in glass jars of varying sizes, glowing with soft, erratic light. There were the words that had gotten stuck on the tips of people’s tongues and were subsequently abandoned when the conversation moved on. They buzzed against the glass like drowsy bumblebees. There were childhood imaginary friends, folded up neatly like origami cranes, waiting patiently to be unfolded. There were the exact melodies of dreams that evaporated the moment a person’s feet touched the bedroom floor.

Arthur loved the second carriage best. At night, sitting in his small office with a cup of tea that never quite went cold, he would sometimes unscrew the lid of a jar just a fraction of an inch. He would inhale the scent of a summer afternoon from 1954—cut grass, coconut sunscreen, and the metallic tang of a rusty bicycle chain—before sealing it tight and placing it on the shelf marked *Ephemera: Unclaimed*.

It was a quiet existence. Lonely, perhaps, if Arthur could remember what company felt like. In truth, he couldn’t recall his own arrival at Terminus Null, nor the life he might have lived before he put on the navy-blue uniform with the silver buttons. He suspected that his own memories were sitting in a jar somewhere in the deep stacks, miles back into the dark, gathering dust. He had never gone looking for them. A good archivist does not tamper with the inventory.

Then came the Tuesday—it felt distinctly like a Tuesday—when the train brought the girl.

The plum-colored doors slid open. The shadow-porters unloaded three crates of mismatched buttons, a tangle of earphones, and forty-two jars of forgotten promises (these always glowed a sickly, bruised violet). Then, from the third carriage—a carriage Arthur had never seen open before—stepped a young woman.

She was wearing an oversized grey sweater and mismatched socks. She looked around the platform, her eyes wide, her breath clouding in the cool, damp air. 

Arthur froze, his hands gripping the brass handle of his cart. 

"Excuse me," she said. Her voice sounded strange in the cavernous station. It had weight. It echoed off the vaulted glass ceiling. "I think I got on the wrong line."

Arthur cleared his throat. It took three tries before a sound came out, dry as dead leaves. "No one gets on this line, miss. Things only fall into it."

She frowned, hugging her arms around her chest. "Well, I’m here. Is there a map? I was trying to get to 42nd Street, and I fell asleep against the window, and when I woke up..." She gestured helplessly at the Pale swirling beyond the tracks.

"Ah," Arthur said, stepping forward slowly, as if approaching a startled deer. "You are dreaming. It happens, once a century or so. A sleeper slips their tether and wanders down the tracks. You shouldn't be here. The air is too thin for the living."

"I don't feel asleep," she murmured, looking past him toward the towering archways of the Great Archive. Her eyes caught the millions of pinpricks of light from the jars stacked into the infinity of the dark. "What is all that?"

"The things you leave behind," Arthur said gently. "Come. Before the train departs. If it leaves without you, waking up becomes... complicated."

He tried to usher her back toward the open doors of the third carriage, where the shadow-porters stood waiting, utterly still. But she pulled away, drawn toward the shelves like a moth to a lantern. 

"Wait," she whispered, walking into the first aisle. "I know that light."

She stopped before a shelf labeled *Recent Displacements*. Her fingers hovered over a small, mason-style jar that pulsed with a warm, amber glow, like firelight through a glass of whiskey. 

"Don't touch that, please," Arthur said, hurrying after her. "It hasn't been cataloged."

"It's my father's laugh," she said, her voice cracking. A tear spilled over her eyelashes, hitting the black-and-white tile with a sharp *clack*, like a falling pebble. "He died three years ago. Yesterday, I realized I couldn't remember what his laugh sounded like. I tried so hard, all day, and it was just... blank. Like a taped-over cassette."

Arthur looked at the jar, then at the girl. He looked at the clock with no hands. Somewhere deep in his chest, beneath the navy-blue wool and the silver buttons, something gave a small, painful tug.

"The rules are very clear," Arthur said softly to the empty air. "Once it is here, it belongs to the Archive."

"Please," she breathed, her hand trembling against the glass.

The train gave its quiet, settling-house sigh. The doors of the first and second carriages slid shut. 

Arthur looked back at the platform, then at the amber jar. With a swift, practiced motion, he reached past her, snatched the jar from the shelf, and pressed it into her hands. The glass was warm. 

"Hold it tight," he instructed, grabbing her by the elbow and steering her rapidly back toward the platform. "Don't open it until you're on the train. Don't look back at me."

"Thank you," she gasped, clutching the jar to her grey sweater. 

They reached the third carriage just as the doors began to close. She slipped inside, turning to face him through the dark glass. Through the window, Arthur watched her unscrew the lid. A burst of golden light flooded the dark interior of the train car, and though the glass was thick, Arthur swore he heard it—a rich, booming, slightly wheezy sound of pure joy. 

The girl smiled, closed her eyes, and vanished into thin air, waking up in a subway car somewhere beneath a city Arthur would never see.

The train glided silently back into the Pale, leaving the platform empty. 

Arthur stood alone by the yellow line for a long time. The station was quiet again, save for the faint buzzing of a thousand forgotten words in their jars. He reached down to the floor where the girl had stood and picked up the tear that had fallen. It had crystallized into a tiny, clear marble, cool to the touch.

He dropped it into his pocket, picked up his birch-twig broom, and walked back into the deep stacks—not to sweep, for once, but to see if he could find a jar with his own name on it.
